body.text: In just six months of the Hindu majoritarian Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) coming to power in West Bengal, the state has witnessed 48 attacks against minority Christians in the state. This is particularly shocking as Bengal, unlike states in northern India, has had a strong tradition of secularism and peaceful coexistence among followers of different faiths.

Documenting such attacks at a hearing in Kolkata on November 2, the People’s Tribunal on Christian Persecutions noted the utter apathy and inaction of the police, who registered complaints in only 16 of the 48 cases. The event was co-hosted by Kolkata-based civil rights groups Sabar Institute and the Aamra Ek Sachetan Prayas.

The Mamata Banerjee-led Trinamool Congress government in Bengal, which was in power for 15 years, was known for its secular rule. However, the BJP, then in opposition in the state, had accused it of appeasing religious minorities, especially Muslims and Christians.
Soon after assuming office on May 4, the BJP and its affiliates lost no time in getting down to business to attack minorities and spread communal hatred.

In a report released in September, the U.S.-based India Hate Lab recorded “60 cases since May 4, comprising 52 coordinated raids on private prayer assemblies and domestic house churches, alongside eight violent mob attacks and explicit instances of physical assault against Christians in West Bengal.” In areas where only a small number of Christians live, prayer assemblies take place in private homes since there is no formal church nearby.

Human rights activist and founder of the New Delhi-based Karwaan-e-Mohabbat (Caravan of Love), Harsh Mander, who spearheaded the People’s Tribunal in Kolkata, pointed out that in just a few months of coming to power, the BJP has started enforcing its national agenda of minority persecution in Bengal as well. “This has never happened in Bengal before,” Mander told The Diplomat.

Drawing attention to a “striking common template” in all these incidents, Mander pointed out that “these attacks are not spontaneous, as is being projected by the administration. These are coordinated strikes against small groups of Christians and not large churches since that will attract [foreign government’s] attention.”
The aim of the attacks is to strike fear in the hearts of Christians, and to socially isolate them.

Christians account for just about 1 percent of West Bengal’s population, but their influence in the socio-cultural life of the state has been far greater. Bengal has had a long colonial past, but Christianity is not perceived as an inimical faith. The state capital, Kolkata, is known for its inclusive and syncretic culture, and Christmas is celebrated by the masses as “Borodin” (Big Day).
However, the BJP’s ideological mentor, the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) has always been wary of Christianity and Christian missionaries, accusing them of carrying out religious conversions.

At the hearing in Kolkata, victims narrated horrifying accounts of the physical violence and terror they had faced. The perpetrators belonged to Hindu supremacist groups like the Vishwa Hindu Parishad, Bajrang Dal, the Hindu Jagran Manch, and Anjani-Putra Sena. Several women recounted how they were physically assaulted, stripped, and had their homes vandalized. Christian priests and pastors told the gathering that Hindutva groups barged into prayer meetings, falsely accusing them of conducting forced conversions. Anup Kumar Ghosh, a priest at a church in Midnapore, was even arrested and kept behind bars for 41 days. In Purba Bardhaman district, a Christian burial was disrupted. The attackers demanded that the body be taken out of the grave. In Kolkata’s suburb of Howrah, an under-construction church was vandalized.

Herod Mullick, founder of the Bangiya Christiya Pariseba (BCP), an interfaith forum representing Christians in the state, rejected the charges that Christians were converting Hindus to Christianity. Mullick told The Indian Express newspaper, “It is a narrative created to portray peaceful Christian gatherings and prayers as instances of forced conversions to justify violence against them.”

Mander, who has been visiting states, including Odisha, that have witnessed a spurt in anti-Christian violence ever since the BJP came to power, says that Odisha has had a history of violence in the past. Anti-Christian violence there in 2008 left 38 dead. However, Bengal has had no such track record, which makes the growing number of Christian attacks “worrisome.”

On November 6, Christian groups, including the All India Christian Council, held a peace march in the heart of Kolkata to protest against attacks and atrocities on Christians and their places of worship in West Bengal.
Article 25 of the Indian Constitution bestows on all citizens the right to profess, practice and propagate their religion freely.

Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari, who heads the BJP government in Bengal, has been using the pretext of religious conversions to deny people the rights granted under Article 25. He is seeking to bring in an anti–conversion law in Bengal. He is not the first to do so. Other BJP state governments have been chipping away at this right for several years.

Adhikari announced in early October that his government is in the process of drafting a Uniform Civil Code (UCC) for Bengal. A controversial legislation, the UCC envisages a single set of laws governing marriage, divorce, inheritance, adoption, and related personal matters for all citizens across all religious communities. Minorities fear that the law is another tool for denying them their religious rights and customs.

This year, for the first time, a Durga Puja, a Hindu festival, was held on Park Street — an area that is synonymous with elaborate Christmas celebrations. It is not a coincidence that the puja was organized by the BJP-backed Sanatani Sangha. The previous Mamata Banerjee government had made the Park Street Christmas celebrations into an annual year-end festival that drew large crowds and tourists. The new BJP government is intent on erasing all traces of secular festivity, which are also contributions of the previous regime.

It is indeed tragic that in Kolkata, which embraced the Albanian Catholic nun Mother Teresa as its own “Mother” for decades, Christians are now under attack and being persecuted by the state government.
